content: In situations where resources are limited, surveillance authorities must strategically allocate these resources to maximize public health benefits. This often involves focusing on areas with higher contamination risks, as indicated by Surveillance Index (SI) scores, Water Safety Plan (WSP) audit scores, or water quality test results. Surface water and shallow groundwater sources are generally more vulnerable to microbial contamination compared to deep groundwater sources. Priority should also be given to water supplies serving healthcare facilities, schools, aged care facilities, and other institutions catering to vulnerable populations. Small water supplies that serve larger populations should be addressed first, with smaller systems being considered as resources permit. Representative sites should be selected for annual surveillance visits to establish trends and inform national and subnational planning. Over time, all sites should be visited on a rotational basis. Sites serving vulnerable populations should also be prioritized. Surveillance agencies should focus on microbial water quality by testing for E. coli. If resources are extremely constrained, monitoring free chlorine residuals in chlorinated supplies should be prioritized, ideally alongside turbidity and pH testing, to ensure optimal conditions for effective chlorination. Presence-absence (P/A) testing can be a cost-effective alternative, particularly in systems where contamination is not expected, such as those maintaining chlorine residuals. P/A testing can also serve as a screening tool to trigger further quantitative testing when contamination is detected. Surveillance staff play a critical role in educating small water suppliers, providing technical support, and encouraging compliance. They must be well-trained not only in water quality sampling and testing but also in water supply design, operations, maintenance, and risk management. Comprehensive training programs should cover topics such as the links between water quality and health, national regulations and standards, water supply types and risks, protective measures, water supply design and operation, WSP processes and audits, sample collection and handling, field testing, data recording and interpretation, and effective communication of results. Training should be ongoing, with refresher courses and field supervision to ensure sustained capacity development. Equipping surveillance staff with well-designed tools and templates, such as those in WHO’s Sanitary Inspection (SI) packages, can enhance their effectiveness. Standardized forms and tools facilitate national and subnational comparisons, risk ranking, and critical thinking about findings and remedial actions. Motivation of surveillance staff is also crucial. Awareness of the impact of their work on improving water safety, along with staff reward programs, can foster a culture of surveillance-driven improvement. Sustainable financing is essential for effective surveillance. Costs include not only direct support but also data management and review to inform programming. For small water supplies, the high number and geographic spread of systems can make surveillance costs significant. While some costs may be covered by user fees, many small systems require dedicated budget allocations to ensure safe and sustainable drinking water services. Combining risk management scores from SIs or WSP audits with microbial water quality data provides a more accurate assessment of water supply safety. This approach helps identify high-risk supplies requiring attention and guides resource allocation and priority setting. Grading schemes based on microbial water quality and risk management scores can support this process. For example, water supplies can be categorized into low, intermediate, high, or very high risk based on E. coli levels and SI or WSP audit scores. These schemes should be adapted to local conditions and designed to balance the distribution of water supplies across risk categories, ensuring effective prioritization of remedial actions.
